maya.name: Maya
signals: followed several new classmates this week
gaming club once · lives on campus

steps.label: COLD OPEN
steps.title: I already made a prediction about you.
steps.lead: Before you answer anything, make a call: could the apps you use every day predict you surprisingly well, or would they get the important parts of you wrong?
choices: PROVE IT — an app could predict me pretty well
NO CHANCE — it would get important things about me wrong
steps.hero: YOUR PHONE HAS BEEN COLLECTING CLUES. TODAY, YOU BECOME THE ALGORITHM.
steps.instructorCue: Do not explain or resolve the vote. Let students see the room split, then say: Good. Today we're going to find out who's right.

runbook.goal: Create curiosity and commitment before students know the framework. The unresolved prediction becomes the narrative thread for the entire session.
runbook.say: Before I explain anything, I want you to make a bet. Could the apps you use every day predict you surprisingly well, or would they get the important parts of you wrong?
runbook.ask: Choose a side silently. No explaining yet: PROVE IT or NO CHANCE?
runbook.watchFor: Do not let this become a debate yet. You want a visible split and genuine curiosity, not resolution.
runbook.advanceWhen: Roughly 80–90% of active students have voted. Lock, reveal the split briefly, then move on while the question is still unresolved.
runbook.ifStuck: Name familiar examples: TikTok For You, Spotify recommendations, Netflix, YouTube, Amazon. Then ask them to vote based on instinct.
runbook.transition: Good. Keep your answer in mind. By the end of class, I’m going to ask whether you still believe it.
runbook.reminder: Do not tell them which side you think is correct. Preserve the tension.

steps.label: RETRIEVE + PERSONALIZE
steps.title: What does your algorithm think you are?
steps.lead: If an app had to describe you using only the traces you leave behind, what is ONE piece of information it could use?
steps.placeholder: One signal an app could use to predict me is…
steps.instructorCue: Give students a minute to respond. Spotlight contrasting examples. Group responses verbally into behavior, identity, social, context, and history.

runbook.goal: Move from abstract AI to students' own digital traces and establish that predictions begin with observable signals.
runbook.say: An app cannot read your mind. It sees traces. What is one trace you leave behind that could become a clue about you?
runbook.ask: Which signals feel harmless? Which begin to feel personal or creepy? Why?
runbook.watchFor: Listen for students treating inferred traits as if they were directly observed. Separate what a platform sees from what it guesses.
runbook.advanceWhen: You have several different signal types represented and at least two contrasting examples to discuss.
runbook.ifStuck: Prompt with: watched, skipped, searched, location, time online, purchases, follows, pauses, device type.
runbook.transition: Those traces are the DATA. But data alone does not produce a recommendation. Something has to turn clues into a prediction.
runbook.reminder: Spotlight responses for variety, not only the most polished answer.

steps.label: TEACH
steps.title: AI is not magic. It is a system.
steps.lead: Use one five-part lens to explain recommendation systems and many other AI systems.
flow:
MODEL / TOOL
patterns learned from examples

HUMAN INTERPRETATION
trust · ignore · question · misunderstand

DECISION / ACTION
click · buy · watch · share · go
steps.instructorCue: Teach one box at a time. Emphasize that pattern is not the same as understanding.

runbook.goal: Give students a reusable five-part mental model they can apply to any AI system, not just recommendation algorithms.
runbook.say: AI feels mysterious when we look only at the output. It becomes easier to reason about when we slow it down into five parts.
runbook.ask: At which point does an AI output actually become consequential?
runbook.watchFor: Students may collapse MODEL and OUTPUT together. Reinforce: the model/tool processes patterns; the output is what it produces.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can verbally trace one familiar recommendation from data through decision/action.
runbook.ifStuck: Use: You watched A, B, C → pattern says people like you often watch D → D appears in For You → you interpret it → you click or ignore.
runbook.transition: Now you know the five parts. Let’s see whether you can build the system yourselves.
runbook.reminder: Keep the mini-lesson moving. This is shared vocabulary, not a lecture on machine-learning math.

steps.label: BUILD THE ALGORITHM
steps.title: You are now the algorithm.
steps.lead: Build VIKING FEED, a fictional system that recommends one thing for Maya to do tonight.
fields: MODEL / TOOL — What patterns should it use?
HUMAN INTERPRETATION — How should Maya read it?
DECISION / ACTION — What could Maya do next?
steps.instructorCue: Show Maya's profile and the four possibilities. Students work alone first, then compare with a neighbor.

runbook.goal: Force students to make the hidden assumptions of a recommendation system explicit before they see the class vote.
runbook.say: You are Viking Feed now. Maya gets one recommendation. Your job is not to guess what I want; your job is to decide what evidence matters and defend the system you build.
runbook.ask: When you and your neighbor disagree, identify exactly where the disagreement entered the five-part system.
runbook.watchFor: Assumptions disguised as data: gaming club once means gamer; pizza orders mean social preference; music taste predicts event choice.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have saved a model and pairs have identified at least one disagreement or assumption.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask: Which three pieces of Maya’s profile would you keep if you had to delete everything else?
runbook.transition: You built the reasoning. Now commit to the output your system would actually produce.
runbook.reminder: Circulate while they work. Collect two assumptions you can call back during the reveal.

steps.label: PREDICT
steps.title: What should Viking Feed recommend?
steps.lead: Based only on Maya’s current profile, make the recommendation. Commit before seeing what the rest of the class chose.
steps.instructorCue: Let the room vote silently. Lock responses once most students have committed. Build suspense before revealing.

runbook.goal: Capture an independent baseline recommendation before discussion or new context influences the room.
runbook.say: No discussion now. Your algorithm has to ship an output. Commit to what Viking Feed should recommend based only on what it knows right now.
runbook.ask: Which option does your system send to Maya?
runbook.watchFor: Participation rate. Do not reveal early; social proof would contaminate the baseline.
runbook.advanceWhen: At least 85% of active students have responded, or the room has clearly stopped moving.
runbook.ifStuck: Remind them that Not enough information is a legitimate system output.
runbook.transition: Locked. Now we can inspect not just what the room chose, but what assumptions produced those choices.
runbook.reminder: Lock before reveal. This baseline powers the changed-minds metric later.

steps.label: REVEAL + CHALLENGE
steps.title: The class has spoken.
steps.lead: Now inspect the recommendation system instead of arguing only about the winning answer.
steps.prompt: What assumptions are hiding behind our recommendations?
steps.instructorCue: Reveal the distribution. Ask someone to defend the least popular choice. Run the assumption test.

runbook.goal: Shift attention from majority answer to reasoning quality and expose the gap between DATA and MEANING.
runbook.say: The winning answer is less interesting than why we produced it. Let’s audit our own algorithm.
runbook.ask: Someone defend the least popular choice. What evidence supports it? Then: what did you infer that Maya’s profile never actually said?
runbook.watchFor: Students using correlation as certainty, single events as identity, or preferences as fixed traits.
runbook.advanceWhen: The class can name at least three assumptions and distinguish an observed signal from an interpretation.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask directly: Does attending gaming club once mean Maya loves gaming? Do two pizza orders mean she wants a pizza social?
runbook.transition: If meaning depends on context, what happens when the context changes?
runbook.reminder: Land clearly on: DATA is not the same as MEANING.

steps.label: UPDATE
steps.title: New information changes everything.
steps.lead: Three new pieces of context just arrived. Recalculate your recommendation.
updates: Gaming club happened because Maya's roommate asked her to go.
Maya has been looking for ways to meet people outside her residence hall.
Maya has a major exam at 8 AM tomorrow.
steps.instructorCue: Reveal the three updates one at a time verbally, pausing after each. Ask students to vote again without discussing first.

runbook.goal: Demonstrate how additional context changes outputs without pretending the model itself suddenly became smarter.
runbook.say: The system just received new context. I’m going to reveal it one piece at a time. Notice when your recommendation begins to move.
runbook.ask: Recalculate silently. What should Viking Feed recommend now?
runbook.watchFor: Changed-minds count and students who refuse to change despite new evidence. Both are useful discussion material.
runbook.advanceWhen: A strong majority of students who voted the first time have voted again so the before/after comparison is meaningful.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask: Which new fact has the highest decision value? Which old signal just became less meaningful?
runbook.transition: Now we can measure something more useful than the winning answer: how much the room moved when the evidence changed.
runbook.reminder: Do not frame changing your mind as being wrong. Frame it as updating from better context.

steps.label: BEFORE vs AFTER
steps.title: The information changed. So did the decision.
steps.lead: Compare the room’s first recommendation with the second. Watch how the room moved when context changed.
steps.hero: NEW DATA → NEW OUTPUT → NEW DECISION. The model did not become more intelligent. The information available to the decision changed.
steps.instructorCue: Use the changed-minds number and side-by-side distributions as the visual centerpiece.

runbook.goal: Make learning visible by showing that changed information can legitimately produce changed judgment.
runbook.say: This is the most important number on the screen: how many of us changed our recommendation after context changed.
runbook.ask: What changed: the data, the model, the output, the human interpretation, the action, or more than one?
runbook.watchFor: Students saying the model became smarter. Redirect toward information quality and system-level reasoning.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can explain the shift using the five-part framework rather than only saying we got more information.
runbook.ifStuck: Point to one student decision path: old signal → old interpretation → new context → revised interpretation → new recommendation.
runbook.transition: If changes can enter anywhere in the system, failures can too. Let’s stress-test it.
runbook.reminder: Pause on the changed-minds metric. This is a signature teaching moment, not a transition screen.

steps.label: FAILURE TEST
steps.title: Find the failure.
steps.lead: Viking Feed makes thousands of recommendations. Where could the greatest risk enter the system?
choices: DATA — missing, wrong, or biased information
MODEL / TOOL — bad patterns or wrong objective
steps.instructorCue: Treat this like a game-show question, then reveal the distribution. Explain that there may not be one correct answer.

runbook.goal: Expand responsible-AI thinking from model bias to whole-system risk.
runbook.say: Now break the system. If Viking Feed causes harm, where could the failure have entered?
runbook.ask: Pick the greatest risk, then prepare to argue why another answer could also be correct.
runbook.watchFor: Students assuming MODEL / TOOL must be the correct answer because it sounds most technical.
runbook.advanceWhen: The room has debated at least two different failure points and recognizes that risk can cascade across the system.
runbook.ifStuck: Give a quick example for each layer: bad data, wrong objective, overconfident output, over-trusting human, harmful action.
runbook.transition: If the whole system can fail, responsibility cannot disappear just because an AI produced the recommendation.
runbook.reminder: There is intentionally no single correct answer. Reward systems thinking.

steps.label: HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY
steps.title: AI recommends. Who is responsible?
steps.lead: Imagine Viking Feed flashes: 97% MATCH — Go to the Pizza Social. Complete the sentence below.
steps.placeholder: Even with AI support, a human still needs to…
steps.instructorCue: Spotlight two or three strong anonymous responses.

runbook.goal: Make human judgment and responsibility explicit after students have seen how uncertain the system can be.
runbook.say: A confident number can make an AI output feel authoritative. But 97% match does not erase human judgment.
runbook.ask: Even with AI support, what does a human still need to do?
runbook.watchFor: Strong verbs: question, verify, contextualize, decide, monitor, challenge, understand consequences.
runbook.advanceWhen: You have spotlighted two or three responses that collectively cover judgment, verification, and consequences.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask: What would you want Maya to remember before treating 97% as an instruction?
runbook.transition: We started class with a bet about whether AI can predict you. Now you have enough evidence to revisit it.
runbook.reminder: Keep responses anonymous when spotlighting unless a student explicitly volunteers.

steps.label: RETURN TO THE PREDICTION
steps.title: So… can AI predict you?
steps.lead: Think back to your first choice: PROVE IT or NO CHANCE. After building and breaking a recommendation system, what would you say now—and what changed your thinking?
steps.placeholder: At the start I thought… Now I think… because…
steps.closing: AI IS NOT MAGIC. It is data, patterns, outputs, people, and decisions.
steps.instructorCue: Explicitly return to the unresolved cold open. Ask whether anyone changed sides and invite one or two explanations.

runbook.goal: Close the narrative loop and have students articulate a more nuanced model of what AI prediction can and cannot mean.
runbook.say: Seventy-five minutes ago I asked you to choose PROVE IT or NO CHANCE. I’m not looking for one correct side now. I’m looking for a better reason.
runbook.ask: Would you choose the same side now? What changed in your reasoning?
runbook.watchFor: Nuance: AI can predict behavioral patterns without fully understanding a person; outputs depend on data, context, and human interpretation.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students have submitted the exit reflection and you have heard one or two examples of changed or strengthened reasoning.
runbook.ifStuck: Use the frame: Before today I thought… Now I think… because…
runbook.transition: Close with the five-part framework and responsibility statement.
runbook.reminder: Final line: AI can support a decision. It does not remove responsibility.
